'''''Commelina communis''''' the '''Asiatic dayflower''', is an [[herbaceous]] [[annual plant]] in the [[Commelinaceae|dayflower family]]. It gets its name because the blooms last for only one day.<ref>{{cite web |title=Asiatic Dayflower Wildflower |url=http://www.wildflowers-guide.com/10-asiatic-dayflower.html |access-date=27 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121101063323/http://www.wildflowers-guide.com/10-asiatic-dayflower.html |archive-date=1 November 2012 }}</ref> It is native throughout much of East Asia and northern parts of Southeast Asia. In China, the plant is known as '''''yazhicao''''' ({{zh|s=[[wikt:鸭|鸭]] [[wikt:跖|跖]] [[wikt:草|草]]|t=鴨跖草|p=yāzhīcǎo}}),<ref name=chinaflora/> roughly translating to "duckfoot herb", while in Japan it is known as {{nihongo|'''''tsuyukusa'''''|[[wikt:露|露]] [[wikt:草|草]]|tsuyukusa}},<ref name=JAANUS/> meaning "dew herb". It has also been introduced to parts of central and southeastern Europe and much of eastern North America, where it has spread to become a [[noxious weed]]. It is common in disturbed sites and in moist soil. The flowers emerge from summer through fall and are distinctive with two relatively large blue petals and one very small white petal.

The Asiatic dayflower plant serves as the [[biological type|type]] species for its large genus. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] picked the name ''Commelina'' in honour of the two Dutch botanists of the Commelijn family, using the two large showy petals of ''Commelina communis'' to symbolise them. Linnaeus described the species in the first edition of his landmark work, ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', in 1753. Long before the plant was studied in Europe, however, it had been used for generations in [[traditional Chinese medicine]]. The flowers have also been used in Japan to produce a dye and a pigment that was used in many world-renowned [[Ukiyo-e]] [[woodblock printing in Japan|woodcuts]] from the 18th and early 19th centuries. In the modern era the plant has found limited use as a [[model organism]] in the field of [[plant physiology]] due to its complex pigment chemistry and the ease of viewing its [[stomata]].

The Asiatic dayflower is considered a weed both in areas where it was introduced and in certain parts of its native range. The flowers' interactions with pollinators have been well studied and have helped to support important hypotheses about pollination in the field of plant ecology. Recent research has also revealed that the Asiatic dayflower can [[Bioaccumulation|bioaccumulate]] a number of metals, making it a candidate for revegetating and essentially [[Phytoremediation|cleaning spoiled copper mines]]. Several animals and fungi use the plant as a food source, with a few species feeding upon it exclusively.

==Description==
[[File:Commelina communis 003.jpg|thumb|left|The [[wikt:spathe|spathe]] at left shows two faded flowers, one on the upper and one on the lower [[wikt:cincinnus|cincinnus]]; the spathe at right has two capsules starting to form on the lower cincinnus; notice the contrasting veins on both spathes]]
The Asiatic dayflower is an annual herb with stems that are typically decumbent, meaning that they are prostrate at the base but become erect towards the tips, but some individuals may be simply erect.<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=flora/> The diffusely branched stems tend to root at the basal [[Node (botany)|nodes]].<ref name=flora/> The pubescence on the stems is variable, but common patterns include a line of hair continuous with the [[leaf sheath]], or they may be [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] basally, meaning hairless, and [[wikt:puberulent|puberulent]] towards the extremities, that is covered with fine hairs.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> The [[leaf|leaves]] are sessile: they lack a leaf stalk, also known as a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]; or they may be subpetiolate, meaning they have very small petioles.<ref name=taiwan/> The leaf sheaths are cylindrical, sometimes striped with red, and typically glabrous, but usually have margins that are puberulent or [[wikt:pilose|pilose]], meaning lined with fine, soft hairs.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> The leaf blades range from narrowly [[lanceolate]], or lance-shaped, to [[Ovate (leaf)|ovate]]–[[Elliptic (leaf shape)|elliptic]], between egg-shaped and ellipse-shaped. They measure {{convert|3|-|12|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} by {{convert|1|-|4|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=flora/> The blades range from glabrous to puberulent and have scabrescent, or slightly rough, margins.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> Their tips are acute, meaning they come to a point quickly, to [[wikt:acuminate|acuminate]], meaning the point develops gradually. The leaf bases are oblique, or uneven.<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=flora/>

The [[flower]]s are arranged on [[inflorescence]]s called cincinni (singular: [[wikt:cincinnus|cincinnus]]), which are also called scorpioid [[Inflorescence#Determinate or cymose|cymes]]. This is a form of a [[wikt:monochasium|monochasium]] where the lateral branches arise alternately. The cincinni are subtended by a [[spathe]], a modified leaf. The solitary spathes usually measure {{convert|1.2|-|3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, but some may be up to {{convert|3.5|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} in length, while they are {{convert|0.8|-|1.3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} tall, but sometimes up to {{convert|1.8|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}}. The uncurved spathes typically have a [[wikt:cordate|cordate]], or heart-shaped, whitish base, which contrasts with its dark green veins. Their margins lack hairs, are somewhat [[wikt:scabrous|scabrous]], or rough, and are unfused, meaning they are distinct to the base. Their apices are acute to acuminate while the surfaces are glabrous, puberulent, or [[wikt:hirsute|hirsute]]–[[wikt:ciliate|ciliate]], meaning with longer, shaggier hairs.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=flora/> The spathes are borne on [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]s, or stalks, that measure {{convert|0.8|-|3.5|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} and sometimes up to {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=flora/>

{{Multiple image

There are often two cincinni present, though the upper, or distal, cincinnus may be [[vestigial]].<ref name=flora/> The lower, or proximal, cincinnus bears 1 to 4 bisexual flowers and is nearly included in the spathe, while the upper cincinnus has 1 to 2 male flowers and is about {{convert|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> The individual flowers are subtended by [[bract]]eoles that fall off early in development. The [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s supporting single flowers, and later the fruits, are erect initially but curve when in fruit. They measure about {{convert|3|-|4|mm|in|abbr=on}}.<ref name=taiwan/> The 3 concave, membranous [[sepal]]s are inconspicuous, but persist after the fruit develops; the lateral pair are fused basally, measure only {{convert|4.5|-|5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|3|-|3.7|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide, and are elliptic and glabrous. The lower sepal is lanceolate and about {{convert|4.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long by about {{convert|2.2|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=taiwan/> The 2 upper [[petal]]s are blue to [[indigo]] in colour, while the much smaller lower petal is white. The upper two petals measure {{convert|9|-|10|mm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|8|-|10|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide, while the lower petal is {{convert|5|-|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} long by about {{convert|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> The 2 upper petals are composed of a claw about {{convert|3|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and a broadly ovate limb with an acute apex and a cuneate-cordate base.<ref name=taiwan/>

There are three anticous fertile [[stamens]], meaning they are on the lower part of the flower, and three posticous infertile stamens, meaning they are on the upper part of the flower. These infertile stamens are termed [[staminode]]s. The fertile stamens are [[Sexual dimorphism|dimorphic]]: the lateral pair have maroon to indigo [[stamen|anther]]s that measure about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and are elliptic with a base that is [[wikt:sagittate|sagittate]] or arrowhead-shaped. Their [[stamen|filament]]s are about {{convert|10|-|12|mm|in|abbr=on}} long. The central fertile stamen has a yellow, elliptic anther with a maroon [[stamen|connective]] and a base that is [[wikt:hastate|hastate]] or spearhead-shaped, but with the lobes at right angles. The anther measures about {{convert|2.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long while its filament is about {{convert|5|-|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=taiwan/> The three staminodes are all alike with yellow, cruciform, or cross-shaped, antherodes that are about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} long on filaments about {{convert|3|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=flora/> Sometimes the antherodes will have a central maroon spot.<ref name=flora/> Each antherode has two abortive lateral pollen sacks. The [[ovary (plant)|ovary]] is [[wikt:ellipsoid|ellipsoid]], about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and has a [[gynoecium|style]] that is about {{convert|1.3|cm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=taiwan/>

The fruit is a [[dehiscent]], ellipsoid [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]] with two [[locule]]s each containing two seeds. The capsule is glabrous, brown, measures {{convert|4.5|-|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, and dehisces into two [[wikt:valve|valves]].<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=flora/> The [[seed]]s are brown or brownish yellow in colour and [[wikt:deltoid|deltoid]], or roughly triangular in outline.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/> They are dorsiventral, meaning they have distinct upper and lower surfaces, with the ventral, or lower, surface being planar and the dorsal, or upper, surface being convex. Seeds range in length from {{convert|2.5|-|4.2|mm|in|abbr=on}}, but seeds as short as {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} can occur, while they are {{convert|2.2|-|3|mm|in|abbr=on}} across. The surfaces are [[wikt:rugose|rugose]] pitted-[[wikt:reticulate|reticulate]] and are densely covered with smaller [[wikt:farinose|farinose]] granules with sparse larger farinose granules.<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=flora/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Commelina communis'' was first described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in the first edition of his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', along with eight other species in the genus.<ref name=flora/><ref>{{citation |title=Species Plantarum |last=Linné |first=Karl von |edition=1 |pages=40–41 |year=1753 |volume=1 |isbn=0-665-55334-X }}</ref> The plant serves as the [[biological type|type]] species for the genus. The scientific name ''Commelina'' was chosen based on the Asiatic dayflower. Linnaeus picked the name in honour of the Dutch botanists [[Jan Commelin|Jan]] and [[Caspar Commelijn]], using the two large showy petals of ''Commelina communis'' to symbolise them.<ref name=flora/> A number of names given to plants thought to be different species have fallen into [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonymy]] with the Asiatic dayflower. [[Albrecht Wilhelm Roth]] created the first such synonym, ''Commelina polygama'', in 1790.<ref name=taiwan/><ref name=mansfeld/> [[Wenceslas Bojer]] described what he believed were two new species, ''Commelina barabata'' and ''Commelina salicifolia'', in his work ''Hortus Mauritianus'', both of which were quickly found to be identical to ''C. communis''.<ref name=mansfeld>{{citation |title=Mansfeld's Encyclopedia of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops |last=Hanelt |first=Peter |author2=Büttner, R. |author3=Mansfeld, Rudolf |author4=Kilian, Ruth |publisher=Springer |year=2001 |isbn=3-540-41017-1 |page=2414 }}</ref> [[Karl Sigismund Kunth]] created the synonym ''Commelina willdenowii'' in 1841.<ref name=mansfeld/> Finally, Korean populations of the species were named under the synonym ''Commelina coreana'' in 1910 by [[Augustin Abel Hector Léveillé]].<ref name=mansfeld/>

Several varieties have also been named. ''Commelina communis'' var. ''ludens'' was created by [[C.B. Clarke]] after demoting it from the full species status in which it was placed by [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel]] in 1861.<ref name=flora/><ref name=mansfeld/> The variety is distinguished by its darker flowers, antherodes with central maroon spots, less well developed distal cymes that usually do not produce a flower, and spathes that are proportionally broader.<ref name=flora/> [[Jisaburo Ohwi]]'s Flora of Japan also treats the variety as geographically distinct, stating that it is restricted to mountainous areas.<ref name=ohwi/> This variety is still accepted by some workers, but others, such Robert B. Faden, consider it impossible to consistently separate from the type variety.<ref name=flora/> Another variety, ''C. communis'' var. ''hortensis'', which was named by [[Tomitaro Makino]] and is apparently a cultivated variety which originated from ''C. communis'' var. ''ludens'' in Japan, is also accepted by some botanists.<ref name=pennell/> It differs in having larger showy flowers which are used to produce a dye (see [[Commelina communis#Uses|"Uses"]] section below).<ref name=ohwi/> A variegated form called ''C. communis'' var. ''ludens'' f. ''aureostriata'' named by Frank C. MacKeever in 1961 is known to occur randomly throughout much of the species' range.<ref name=flora/>

==Distribution and habitat==
The plant's native distribution includes much of East Asia and Southeast Asia. Country by country, it is found in China, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, the [[Russian Far East]], Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Thailand, India, Iran and Vietnam. Within China it is found in all provinces except Qinghai, Hainan, Xinjiang, and Tibet.<ref name=chinaflora>{{Citation |last=Hong |first=Deyuan |author2=DeFillipps, Robert A. |contribution=Commelina communis |year=2000 |title=Flora of China |editor-last=Wu |editor-first=Z. Y. |editor2=Raven, P.H. |editor3=Hong, D.Y. |volume=24 |page=36 |place=Beijing |publisher=Science Press; St. Louis: Missouri Botanical Garden Press |contribution-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200027375 |isbn=962-209-437-6 }}</ref> In Japan the plant is found throughout the bulk of the country from [[Hokkaido]] south to [[Kyūshū]]. In Russia the Asiatic dayflower is found naturally on [[Sakhalin]] as well as in the [[Russian Far East|Far East]] in areas surrounding the [[Ussuri River]].<ref name=ohwi>{{citation |title=Flora of Japan (in English) |last=Ohwi |first=Jisaburo |year=1965 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |location=Washington, D.C. |page=271 |isbn=0-87474-708-2 }}</ref>

The species has been introduced to much of Europe and eastern North America. On the former continent it is now found from Central Europe well into western Russia.<ref name=taiwan>{{citation |last=Hsu |first=K.C. |editor-last=Li |title=Flora of Taiwan |contribution=Commelina communis |volume=5 |page=164 |year=1978 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=100&taxon_id=200027375 |display-editors=etal }}</ref> Specifically it is known from Italy north to Switzerland, east through the region encompassing the former [[Yugoslavia]], east into the regions around the [[Black Sea]] including Romania, the [[Moldavia|Moldavia Region]], and Ukraine but excluding [[Crimea]], north through the [[Dnieper River|Dnieper Basin]] into Belarus and Russia, continuing east into the regions surrounding the [[Don River (Russia)|Don River]] and the [[Volga River]] south to their intersection at the [[Volga–Don Canal]] and north to the regions around [[Lake Ladoga]] and [[Lake Ilmen]], and farther east to the regions of the [[Ural River]] and the [[Kama River]]. It is also found in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.<ref>{{citation |title=Flora Europaea |contribution-url=http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Commelina&SPECIES_XREF=communis&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK=species |isbn=978-0-521-80570-4 |year=1980 |contribution=Commelinaceae |volume=5 |editor1=Tutin, T.G. |editor2=V. H. Heywood |editor3=N. A. Burges |editor4=D. H. Valentine |editor5=S. M. Walters |editor6=D. A. Webb |publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref> It is present in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec in Canada, and in most of the eastern and central American states from Massachusetts and New York state in the northeast, west to Minnesota and south through the [[Great Plains]] to Texas and east to Florida in the United States.<ref name=flora>{{Citation |last=Faden |first=Robert |contribution=Commelina communis |year=2006 |title=Flora of North America |volume=22 |page=193 |contribution-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200027375 |place=New York & Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press }}</ref>

Within its native distribution, the plant is most typical of moist, open places, including shady forest edges and wet areas of crop fields, orchards, ditches, and roadsides.<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=taiwan/><ref>{{Citation |last=Hong |first=Deyuan |title=''Commelina'' Linn. |year=1997 |encyclopedia=Flora Reipublicae Popularis Sinicae |editor=Wu Kuofang |volume=13 |pages=125–133 |location=Beijing |publisher=Science Press |isbn=7-03-005367-2 |issue=3 |language=zh }}</ref> In Taiwan, it can be found from {{convert|350|to|2400|m|ft|abbr=on}} elevation.<ref name=taiwan/> In areas where the Asiatic dayflower is an introduced weed it is most common in waste places, but also along the edges of fields, woods, and marshes, and occasionally penetrating into woods.<ref name=flora/>

==Ecology==
<!-- Unsourced image removed: [[File:Commelina communis.JPG|thumb|right|The Asiatic dayflower growing as a weed along pavement in Massachusetts|{{Deletable image-caption|1=Friday, 24 April 2009|date=May 2012}}]] -->
The Asiatic dayflower is considered an [[invasive plant|invasive]] weed in many areas where it has been introduced. In the United States, the [[Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation]], for example, categorises the species as "occasionally invasive" in its ''Invasive Plant Species of Virginia''. This means that the plant will "not affect ecosystem processes, but may alter plant community composition by outcompeting one or more native plant species". The species is typically limited to disturbed sites, whence it spreads relatively slowly.<ref>{{citation |publisher=Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, Division of Natural Heritage |year=2003 |url=http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/documents/invlist.pdf |title=Invasive Plant Species of Virginia |access-date=29 August 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512084245/http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/documents/invlist.pdf |archive-date=12 May 2008 }}</ref> Within its native range in China it is also sometimes considered a pest, especially in the northeast of the country where it has caused economically significant agricultural damage in orchards.<ref name=chinainvade>{{Citation |last=Zheng |first=Hao |author2=Wu, Yun |author3=Ding, Jianqing |author4=Binion, Denise |author5=Fu, Weidong |author6=Reardon, Richard |title=''Commelina communis'' |work=Invasive Plants of Asian Origin Established in the United States and Their Natural Enemies, Volume 1 |publisher=USDA Forest Service |date=September 2004 |url=http://www.invasive.org/weeds/asian/commelina.pdf |access-date=6 June 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060928013326/http://www.invasive.org/weeds/asian/commelina.pdf |archive-date=28 September 2006 }}</ref>

The Asiatic dayflower has been used in [[pollination]] studies concerning the behaviour of plants in relation to their pollinators. One important experiment tested the hypotheses that floral guides (i.e. various patterns and colours on anthers and petals) simultaneously promote pollinator visitation and prevent visits where the pollinator fails to come into contact with the stigma or [[anther]]s, termed pollen theft. As the flowers of the Asiatic dayflower lack nectar, they offer only pollen as a reward to their visitors. To attract pollinators, the plant has three types of brightly colored floral organs: the large blue petals, fertile yellow anthers, and infertile yellow antherodes that lack pollen. When the infertile antherodes were experimentally removed in natural populations, the number of total floral visitor landings was reduced, supporting the hypothesis that these infertile anthers essentially trick their pollinators into believing they offer more than they actually do. When the central, bright yellow fertile anther was removed, leaving only two brown fertile anthers, the frequency of legitimate flower landings decreased, meaning that the visitors were not pollinating the flowers, suggesting that floral signals also prevent "theft", or visits where the pollinators take pollen, but do not place any on the stigma. Thus both the fertile anthers and the infertile antherodes were shown to play an important role in both increasing visitor landings and orienting floral visitors toward a landing point appropriate for pollination.<ref name=japan>{{citation |title=Colored floral organs influence pollinator behavior and pollen transfer in ''Commelina communis'' (Commelinaceae) |last1=Ushimaru |first1=Atushi |journal=American Journal of Botany |pages=249–258 |year=2007 |doi=10.3732/ajb.94.2.249 |volume=94 |issue=2 |last2=Watanabe |first2=T. |last3=Nakata |first3=K. |pmid=21642227 |bibcode=2007AmJB...94..249U |hdl=20.500.14094/90001107 |url=http://www.lib.kobe-u.ac.jp/repository/90001107.pdf }}</ref>
[[File:Hoverfly April 2008-3.jpg|thumb|right|A male syrphid fly, ''[[Episyrphus balteatus]]'', the most common pollinator of the Asiatic dayflower in much of its range]]
Recent studies have shown that wild Asiatic dayflower populations found growing on [[copper mine]] spoils in eastern China exhibited very high concentrations of copper within the plants, the highest in the 48 species tested. ''Commelina communis'' had sequestered some 361 mg/kg of copper, while the plant with the next highest concentration, ''[[Polygonum]] macrathum'', had 286 mg/kg. Five of the species examined, including the Asiatic dayflower, also showed high concentrations of other metals such as [[zinc]], lead, and [[cadmium]]. The results suggest that the Asiatic dayflower is a good candidate for copper mine spoil revegetation and phytoremediation.<ref>{{citation |title=Bioaccumulation of Heavy Metals by Wild Plants Growing on Copper Mine Spoils in China |last1=Xiao |first1=W.L. |journal=Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis |volume=39 |pages=315–328 |year=2008 |doi=10.1080/00103620701826415 |issue=3 & 4 |last2=Luo |first2=C. L. |last3=Chen |first3=Y. H. |last4=Shen |first4=Z. G. |last5=Li |first5=X. D. |bibcode=2008CSSPA..39..315X |s2cid=94992325 |hdl=10397/33733 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Ten species of fungi have been found on the Asiatic dayflower, four of which can infect the plant, while 12 species of insects are known to be associated with it. Two of the fungi, ''[[Kordyana commelinae]]'' and ''[[Phyllosticta commelinicola]]'', are thought to be host specific with the Asiatic dayflower. Of the ten fungi seven are [[Basidiomycota]] and three are [[Ascomycota]]. Nine of the 12 insects associated with the plant are [[beetle]]s, seven of which are in the genus ''Lema'', while the other two are in the families [[Hispidae]] and [[Pentatomidae]]. The remaining three insects include one species of [[moth]], ''[[Pergesa acteus]]'', and two [[true bugs]], namely ''[[Aphis]] commilinae'' and ''[[Aeschrocoris ceylonicus]]''.<ref name=chinainvade/> Important pollinators include the Asian honeybee, ''[[Apis cerana]]'', syrphid fly, ''[[Episyrphus balteatus]]'', and the bumble bee species ''[[Bombus]] diversus''.<ref name=japan/>

==Uses==

===Medicine and food===
[[File:Suzuki Harunobu 001.jpg|thumb|right|Ukiyo-e woodcut by [[Suzuki Harunobu]]; the blue pigment used on the [[kimono]] is believed to be ''aigami'' made from petals of the Asiatic dayflower; the alternative would be ''ai'' derived from ''[[Polygonum tinctorum]]'']] In China it is used as a medicinal herb with [[febrifuge|febrifugal]], [[antipyretic]], [[anti-inflammatory]], and [[diuretic]] effects. Additionally, it is also used for treating sore throats and [[tonsillitis]].<ref name=chinaflora/><ref name=mansfeld/> Recent pharmacological investigations have revealed that the Asiatic dayflower contains at least five active compounds. One of these, p-hydroxycinnamic acid, shows antibacterial activity, while another, D-mannitol, has an [[antitussive]] effect.<ref>{{citation |last1=Tang |first1=XY |title=Active constituents of ''Commelina communis'' L. |journal=Zhongguo Zhong Yao Za Zhi |volume=19 |pages=297–298 |year=1994 |issue=5 |pmid=7945872 |last2=Zhou |first2=MH |last3=Zhang |first3=ZH |last4=Zhang |first4=YB |language=zh }}</ref> In China and India the plant is also used as a vegetable and [[fodder]] crop.<ref name=mansfeld/>

===Pigment and dye===
In Japan there is a sizeable dye industry devoted to the plant. The purported variety ''Commelina communis'' var. ''hortensis'', which is apparently a cultivated form of another putative variety, namely ''Commelina communis'' var. ''ludens'', is grown for its larger petals which yield a blue juice used in manufacturing a paper called ''boshigami'' or {{nihongo|''aigami''|[[wikt:藍|藍]] [[wikt:紙|紙]]}},<ref name=JAANUS/> which is the famous product of the Yamada village in the [[Shiga prefecture]].<ref name=pennell>{{Citation |last=Pennell |first=Francis W. |author-link=Francis W. Pennell |title=What Is Commelina Communis? |journal=Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia |volume=90 |year=1938 |pages=31–39 }}</ref> The paper is usually resoaked, allowing the pigment to be reabsorbed in water for use as a dye.<ref name=JAANUS/> The dye, also referred to as ''aigami'', but also as {{nihongo|''aobanagami''|[[wikt:青|青]] [[wikt:花|花]] [[wikt:紙|紙]]}} or {{nihongo|''tsuyukusairo''|露草[[wikt:色|色]]}},<ref name=JAANUS>{{citation |title=Japanese Architecture and Art Net User System |contribution=Aigami 藍紙 |last=Parent |first=Mary Neighbour |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/a/aigami.htm |year=2001 }}</ref> is composed primarily of malonyl awobanin and was used extensively as a colorant in 18th and 19th century [[woodblock print]]s in Japan, especially during the early [[Ukiyo-e]] era.<ref>{{Citation |last=Whitmore |first=Paul M. |author2=Cass, Glen R. |title=The Ozone Fading of Traditional Japanese Colorants |journal=Studies in Conservation |volume=33 |year=1988 |pages=29–40 |doi=10.2307/1506238 |issue=1 |jstor=1506238 }}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=Non-Destructive Identification of Blue Colorants in Ukiyo-e Prints by Visible-Near Infrared Reflection Spectrum Obtained with a Portable Spectrophotometer Using Fiber Optics |first=Susumu |author1=Shimoyama |author2=Matsui, Hideo |author3=Shimoyama, Yasuko |journal=Bunseki Kagaku |volume=55 |year=2006 |doi=10.2116/bunsekikagaku.55.121 |page=121 |issue=2 |language=ja |doi-access=free }}</ref> The colorant is known to have been used by several famous Ukiyo-e artists such as [[Torii Kiyonaga]].<ref>{{citation |last=Hirano |first=Chie |title=Kiyonaga, a Study of his Life and Times |year=1939 |location=Boston |pages=38–41 }}</ref> However, ''aigami'' fades to a greenish yellow in a matter of months when exposed to sunlight. As a result, the color was eventually replaced by imported [[Prussian blue]], a much more stable colour with its first commercial appearance in 1829 in the work of [[Keisai Eisen]].<ref>{{citation |title=Japanese Woodblock Prints: A Catalogue of the Mary A. Ainsworth Collection |first=Roger |last=Keyes |publisher=Allen Memorial Art Museum, Oberlin College |year=1984 |pages=42, 91, 185 |isbn=0-942946-01-4 }}</ref> The plant is also grown for its dye in northern China.<ref name=mansfeld/> Additional uses of the colourant include making preparatory designs on cloth before dyeing with other pigments.<ref name=JAANUS/>

[[Commelinin]], the blue pigment from the flowers of ''C. communis'', is a [[metalloanthocyanin]]. It is a complex of 4 [[Magnesium|Mg]]<sup>2+</sup> ions chelating six anthocyanin molecules.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2183/pjab.84.452 |vauthors=Shiono M, Matsugaki N, Takeda K |title=Structure of commelinin, a blue complex pigment from the blue flowers of ''Commelina communis'' |journal=Proc. Jpn. Acad., Ser. B, Phys. Biol. Sci. |volume=84 |issue=10 |pages=452–6 |year=2008 |pmid=19075517 |pmc=3720548 |bibcode=2008PJAB...84..452S }}</ref>

===Plant physiology and development===
''Commelina communis'' is also used as a [[model organism]] in [[plant physiology]] and [[plant development]] to a limited extent, especially in relation to [[stomata|stomatal physiology]] and the biology of pigmentation development.<ref name=taiz>{{citation |title=Plant Physiology |last=Taiz |first=Lincoln |author2=Zieger, Eduardo |edition=4 |publisher=Sinauer |location=Sunderland, Massachusetts |isbn=0-87893-856-7 |year=2006 |pages=326, 451, 604, 605 }}</ref> For example, the blue pigmentation of Asiatic dayflower petals was shown to consist of a large complex of six [[anthocyanin]]s, six [[flavones]], and two associated magnesium ions, demonstrating that supramolecular complexes of several copigments and [[chelation|chelated]] metals often determine colour.<ref>{{citation |title=Structural basis of blue-color development in flower petals from ''Commelina communis'' |journal=Nature |volume=358 |pages=515–518 |year=1992 |last1=Kondo |first1=T. |doi=10.1038/358515a0 |last2=Yoshida |first2=Kumi |last3=Nakagawa |first3=Atsushi |last4=Kawai |first4=Takatoshi |last5=Tamura |first5=Hirotoshi |last6=Goto |first6=Toshio |issue=6386 |bibcode=1992Natur.358..515H |s2cid=4288712 }}</ref> Other research on the plant has helped to explain [[photoreception|photoreceptor systems]] in plants such as their stomatal responses to blue light versus red light spectrums,<ref name=taiz/><ref>{{citation |last1=Schwartz |first1=A. |year=1984 |title=Metabolic energy for stomatal opening. Roles of photophosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation |journal=Planta |volume=161 |pages=129–136 |doi=10.1007/BF00395472 |last2=Zeiger |first2=E. |issue=2 |pmid=24253600 |bibcode=1984Plant.161..129S |s2cid=12539218 }}</ref> [[abscisic acid]] perception and its role in cell signaling, particularly concerning the chemical's role in stomatal function,<ref name=taiz/><ref>{{citation |last1=Allan |first1=A.C. |year=1994 |title=Two Transduction Pathways Mediate Rapid Effects of Abscisic Acid in Commelina Guard Cells |journal=Plant Cell |volume=6 |pages=1319–1328 |doi=10.1105/tpc.6.9.1319 |pmid=12244274 |last2=Fricker |first2=MD |last3=Ward |first3=JL |last4=Beale |first4=MH |last5=Trewavas |first5=AJ |issue=9 |pmc=160523 }}</ref><ref>{{citation |last1=Anderson |first1=B.E. |year=1994 |title=Evidence for an Extracellular Reception Site for Abscisic Acid in Commelina Guard Cells |journal=Plant Physiology |volume=104 |pages=1177–1183 |pmid=12232155 |last2=Ward |first2=JM |last3=Schroeder |first3=JI |issue=4 |pmc=159278 |doi=10.1104/pp.104.4.1177 }}</ref> the role of [[vanadate]]s in inhibiting stomatal opening,<ref>{{citation |last1=Schwartz |first1=Amnon |title=Vanadate inhibition of stomatal opening in epidermal peels of ''Commelina communis'' |journal=Planta |year=1991 |volume=183 |pages=590–596 |doi=10.1007/BF00194281 |last2=Illan |first2=Nitza |last3=Assmann |first3=Sarahm. |issue=4 |pmid=24193853 |s2cid=33134013 }}</ref> and the necessity of calcium in stomatal closure,<ref>{{citation |title=Calcium Effects on Stomatal Movement in ''Commelina communis'' L.: Use of EGTA to Modulate Stomatal Response to Light, KCl and CO2 |last1=Schwartz |first1=Amnon |journal=Plant Physiology |year=1988 |volume=87 |pages=583–587 |doi=10.1104/pp.87.3.583 |pmid=16666189 |last2=Ilan |first2=N |last3=Grantz |first3=DA |issue=3 |pmc=1054802 }}</ref> among other topics. Its widespread use in stomatal studies is due to the fact that the leaves produce exceptional epidermal peels that are consistently one cell layer thick. This same quality makes the plant popular for use in laboratory exercises in higher education for demonstrating stomatal function and morphology. [[Guard cell]] [[turgor pressure]] and its regulation in the opening and closing of stomata is particularly easy to demonstrate with the Asiatic dayflower.<ref>{{citation |last=Weyers |first=J.D.B. |year=1994 |title=Investigating stomatal physiology with epidermal strips from ''Commelina communis'' L. (Dayflower) |journal=Journal of Biological Education |volume=28 |pages=255–259 |issue=4 |doi=10.1080/00219266.1994.9655402 }}</ref>
